newsitem.title: UK: UK millionaire's Nepalese heir faces deportation.
newsitem.headline: UK millionaire's Nepalese heir faces deportation.

text.p: A young Nepalese man brought to Britain by a millionaire who made him heir to his fortune lost a four-year legal battle on Thursday against a deportation order.
A High Court judge ruled that interior minister Michael Howard had been right to order the deportation of Jay Kadkha, 20, although he agreed the decision might seem harsh.
"I am unable to conclude that the secretary of state's decision in this case was beyond the range of responses open to a reasonable decision-maker," Judge John Laws said.
Computer tycoon Richard Morley brought Kadkha to Britain in 1990, honouring a pact he made with the boy's father.
Basu Kadkha, a policeman in a remote area of Nepal, saved Morley's life when the millionaire collapsed with a punctured lung while on a mountaineering expedition in Nepal in 1988.
The policeman ran 60 miles (100 km) to the nearest telephone to summon help, but refused financial reward, instead imploring Morley to take care of his son if anything should happen to him.
Morley returned to Nepal in 1990 to find that the elder Kadkha had died two years earlier and that his 14-year-old son was working in a stone quarry.
He brought Kadkha back to Britain and made him his sole heir to an inheritance that included a castle in the English county of Gloucestershire and apartments in London and on England's south coast.
But he was unable to adopt him because of problems with the boy's passport and Britain's interior ministry ruled that he must leave the country.
Morley had argued that Kadkha, who now speaks fluent English and is studying to go to university, would be unable to adjust to life in his former homeland.
Kadkha has been living with Morley in a community in the castle in central England. Under the community's rules, Jay is forbidden to marry outside the "family".
Laws agreed that the ruling "may appear harsh."
"He is not only surrounded by love and affection, which he plainly returns, but is also held in high regard as a fine young man," he said in his written ruling.
But he said it was not his position to overturn Howard's ruling on compassionate grounds.
"If I were to overturn it, I would usurp that role, which it is no business of mine to do. And it goes without saying that my personal view of the case's merits has no relevance whatever," Laws said.
